# 10.16 — Newton's method for a convex-concave game

## Problem and experiment coverage

This is an original solution to the numerical exercise on printed page 560
of [Boyd and Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization*](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf#page=574),
using the payoff in equation (10.32), printed page 542. It includes random
problem generation, explicit Newton steps, residual and step-length plots, and
a crossed experiment over three backtracking choices and three starting-point
radii. No requested component is omitted.

The minimizing player chooses $`u`$, the maximizing player chooses $`v`$, and

```math
f(u,v)=u^TAv+b^Tu+c^Tv-\log(1-u^Tu)+\log(1-v^Tv),
\qquad \|u\|_2<1,\ \|v\|_2<1.
```

We use $`p=q=100`$, matching the dimensions of the book's example. A seeded
local generator draws independent $`A_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(0,1/q)`$,
$`b_i,c_j\sim\mathcal N(0,1)`$. These distributions specify a reproducible
instance; the book does not prescribe a unique random draw.

## Residual and Jacobian

With $`s_u=1-u^Tu`$, $`s_v=1-v^Tv`$, stationarity is

```math
r(u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}Av+b+2u/s_u\\ A^Tu+c-2v/s_v\end{bmatrix}=0.
```

Define

```math
H_u=2I/s_u+4uu^T/s_u^2,\qquad
H_v=2I/s_v+4vv^T/s_v^2.
```

Then the residual Jacobian is the symmetric indefinite matrix

```math
J=\begin{bmatrix}H_u&A\\ A^T&-H_v\end{bmatrix}.
```

The code solves $`J\Delta z=-r`$ directly using a symmetric linear solve.
An SPD elimination is also possible: solve with $`H_u`$, then with the
Schur complement $`H_v+A^TH_u^{-1}A`$. Unlike a convex minimization Hessian,
$`J`$ itself must **not** be treated as positive definite.

Both $`H_u\succeq2I`$ and $`H_v\succeq2I`$, so the game is strongly
convex-concave. Its saddle point is unique. Negating the second residual block
would give a strongly monotone operator; the Newton direction and residual norm
are unchanged by that consistent sign convention.

## Residual line search and starts

Starting from $`t=1`$, we multiply by $`\beta`$ until both trial strategies
are strictly inside their unit balls and

```math
\|r(z+t\Delta z)\|_2\le(1-\alpha t)\|r(z)\|_2.
```

We use a residual merit function; the saddle payoff itself is not expected to
monotonically increase or decrease. Termination requires residual at most
$`10^{-10}`$, and hitting the iteration limit or failing the line search
raises an error instead of returning a false convergence result.

Two random unit directions are generated with a separate local seed. Their
radii are 0, 0.75, and 0.97, crossed with
$`(\alpha,\beta)=(0.01,0.5),(0.1,0.5),(0.25,0.8)`$.
Thus all nine starts satisfy the domain requirement, including the near-boundary
case. Within each radius group, only the line-search parameters change.

## Independent saddle-point checks

There is a useful closed-form best response that does not use the implemented
Hessian. For fixed $`v`$, set $`a=Av+b`$; for fixed $`u`$, set
$`d=A^Tu+c`$. Then

```math
u_{\rm br}=-\frac{a}{1+\sqrt{1+\|a\|^2}},\qquad
v_{\rm br}=\frac{d}{1+\sqrt{1+\|d\|^2}}.
```

These follow by solving each player's radial stationarity equation and always
lie inside the unit ball. We independently solve the best-response fixed-point
equations with SciPy's finite-difference `root` method. The measured agreement
with the Newton solutions is included below.

At each computed point, the code also evaluates the nonnegative saddle gap

```math
f(u,v_{\rm br})-f(u_{\rm br},v).
```

The measured gaps are included below. Tests separately verify the
payoff gradient and full indefinite Hessian by finite differences, line-search
contraction at every accepted step, and the global saddle inequalities under
independent random unilateral deviations.

# Exercise 11.1 — A barrier central path

**Source:** Boyd and Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization*, exercise 11.1, printed p. 623 ([official book](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf)). This is an original derivation and implementation.

## Solution

For the two inequalities $`2-x\le0`$ and $`x-4\le0`$, the logarithmic barrier is

```math
\phi(x)=-\log(x-2)-\log(4-x),\qquad 2<x<4.
```

At a fixed positive $`t`$, the centering objective is

```math
F_t(x)=t(x^2+1)-\log(x-2)-\log(4-x).
```

Its derivatives are

```math
F_t'(x)=2tx-\frac1{x-2}+\frac1{4-x},\qquad
F_t''(x)=2t+\frac1{(x-2)^2}+\frac1{(4-x)^2}>0.
```

Consequently there is exactly one central point. It is the root of

```math
tx(x-2)(4-x)+x-3=0
```

in $`(2,4)`$. We find that root with a bracketed scalar solver, rather than choosing among the three roots of a cubic. Because the derivative at $`x=3`$ is $`6t>0`$, the root belongs to $`(2,3)`$. It decreases toward the constrained optimum $`x^\star=2`$ as $`t\to\infty`$, and tends to the interval's analytic center, 3, as $`t\downarrow0`$.

The multipliers recovered from a central point are

```math
\lambda_1=\frac1{t(x-2)},\qquad \lambda_2=\frac1{t(4-x)}.
```

They satisfy stationarity $`2x-\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0`$, and their complementarity sum is $`2/t`$. Thus $`f_0(x^\star(t))-5\le2/t`$.

## Reproduce and inspect

Run `convex-solutions run 11.1 --output artifacts/11.1 --seed 0` from the repository root. Direct Python use is `ex_11_1.solve(Path("artifacts/11.1"))`.

`barrier_central_path.png` includes the original objective and five separate centering plots, for $`t=0.05,0.2,1,5,25`$. Each panel labels its own $`x^\star(t)`$; separate vertical scales avoid hiding the small-$`t`$ curves. `results.json` records the central points, stationarity residuals, objective gaps, and theoretical bounds.

Tests check strict interiority, monotonic approach to 2, the derivative equation, and the gap inequality. A nonpositive $`t`$ is rejected.

# Exercise 9.31 — Approximate Newton directions

**Source:** Boyd and Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization*, Exercise 9.31, printed pp. 519–520 ([official book](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf#page=533)). This original solution implements both approximations and compares them with gradient descent and exact Newton on the analytic-centering instances from [9.30](9.30.md).

## Common setup

All methods begin at zero. Every accepted step is strictly feasible and satisfies Armijo backtracking with $`\alpha=0.1,\beta=0.5`$. For a fair comparison, **all methods use the identical stopping criterion** $`\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\le10^{-7}`$. This differs intentionally from the method-specific stopping criteria in Exercise 9.30, so its Newton iteration counts need not be identical.

The three matrix sizes are $`(m,n)=(30,10),(100,30),(300,100)`$, with independent standard normal entries and seeds 0, 1, and 2. A high-accuracy Newton solution supplies reference values, while $`\|\nabla f\|^2/4`$ bounds suboptimality independently of the approximation used.

## (a) Reuse a Hessian and its factorization

For each $`N\in\{2,5,10,20\}`$, refresh $`H=\nabla^2 f(x_k)`$ and its Cholesky factors whenever $`k`$ is a multiple of $`N`$, including $`k=0`$. On intervening iterations use the stored factors to solve $`Hd=-\nabla f(x_k)`$. The matrix is stale, but remains positive definite, so

```math
\nabla f(x_k)^Td=-\nabla f(x_k)^TH^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)<0
```

away from stationarity. Consequently feasible backtracking can still find a decreasing step. The code counts actual Hessian evaluations and factorizations; it does not secretly recompute the current Hessian during reuse steps.

For dense $`A`$, a refresh costs roughly $`O(mn^2+n^3)`$. Other iterations require gradient computation, line search, and an $`O(n^2)`$ triangular solve. Increasing $`N`$ therefore trades fewer factorizations for less accurate search directions and potentially more iterations.

## (b) Use only the Hessian diagonal

With $`s=1-Ax`$, the required entries are

```math
D_{jj}=\sum_i A_{ij}^2/s_i^2+\frac{2(1+x_j^2)}{(1-x_j^2)^2}.
```

Compute this vector directly in $`O(mn)`$, without constructing the dense Hessian, and take $`d_j=-g_j/D_{jj}`$. Each diagonal entry is positive, so the direction is again a strict descent direction away from the optimum. This is a coordinate-scaled gradient method; it corrects unequal coordinate scales but ignores cross-coordinate curvature.

## Interpreting work counts

The executed comparison below reports accepted updates and actual Cholesky
factorizations for all methods, along with the final gradient residuals and
feasibility diagnostics. Diagonal and gradient methods use no Cholesky
factorization. Reusing a Hessian saves factorizations, at the price of more
updates. The diagonal method's relative performance depends on the instance.
This is an instance-dependent observation; the experiment does not claim a universal wall-clock speed ordering. Factorization counts omit gradients, line searches, and solves, and therefore are a structural cost measure rather than a timing benchmark.

## Reproduce and validate

```python
from pathlib import Path
from convex_solutions.chapters.ch09.ex_9_31 import run_experiment
result = run_experiment(Path("artifacts/9.31"), seed=0)
# periods and dimensions are configurable.
```

`solve(output_dir=None, seed=0)` is the repository entry point. `results.json` stores objective/gap/gradient/step histories, margins, and work counts for every run. Tests compare the direct diagonal formula to the full Hessian, verify convergence and feasibility of both approximations, check the exact refresh count, and show that reuse with period one reproduces exact Newton step for step.

See the [execution record](../../coverage/results-refresh.json) for the exact command, package versions, source fingerprint, and checks.

All **21** recorded statuses are
**converged**. The shared stopping tolerance is checked by the
actual final norms below, rather than inferred from update counts.

The gradient-based bound is computed from each recorded final norm as
$`\|\nabla f\|_2^2/4`$. Positive trajectory margins confirm strict feasibility.
Full final optimizers (including all 100 coordinates of the largest instance),
objective histories, step lengths, backtracks, and actual Hessian/diagonal
work counts are preserved in the JSON.

Hessian reuse reduces factorization counts while increasing accepted updates.
The diagonal approximation is faster in update count than gradient descent
on the smallest and largest instances, but slower on the middle one; no
universal wall-clock speed ranking follows from these counts.
